#10810. Why ‘you don’t have to use AI’ is the new AI pitch

Watching Adobe’s keynote presentation at the 24th annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope the software giant is walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through. In both cases, there’s a desire to be AI-forward and skate to where the puck is going. At the same time, they need to deal with a hostile crowd—meaning the growing backlash against AI among many of their customers.

At Adobe’s last two annual Max events, AI was a huge emphasis. The company touted AI features, including ways to generate content directly in its Creative Cloud apps, such as Photoshop and Premiere. Adobe hyped up Firefly, which was then mostly associated with the company’s image models. In 2024, Adobe told the audience that “2024 will go down as the year that creativity changed forever.” In 2025, the headliners were a new Firefly image model and a lineup of third-party models from Google, OpenAI, Runway, and others, and “choice” mostly meant choosing which AI model to use. The lone nod to skeptics was a passing aside: “Of course, you can ignore it all as well.”

This year, the tone shifted. In fact, one of the first things incoming CEO Anil Chakravarthy emphasized during the opening keynote was that users didn’t have to use AI if they didn’t want to. “Some of you don’t want to have anything to do with AI,” he said, promising to give those users “the precision and control that you’re looking for, and the option to not use AI.”


Instead of a new Firefly model number, the keynote spotlighted upgrades with no AI in them at all, like a rebuilt color mode in Premiere and Dynamic Text in Illustrator. Firefly is still an area of focus, but it’s evolved into a catch-all creative studio, more like Figma than an AI model. (Disclosure: Adobe paid for my travel to the Max conference, though it had no input on this column.)

AI-optional doesn’t mean AI-free

None of this is to say Adobe is walking away from AI. Far from it: During that same keynote, Chakravarthy announced Adobe would be providing a way for AI services to access Creative Cloud applications directly through the model context protocol (MCP) standard. That means AI users will be able to have Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini act as an agent, effectively “driving” Photoshop and other Creative Cloud apps to edit projects, create content, and export files directly on their computers. The integrations go into private beta testing in early 2027.

Adobe already provides an AI connector that works similarly, but the MCPs would take things to a new level of precision and control. Jesus Diaz has a great breakdown of exactly how they would work and what it means for creators. In addition, Adobe is building out its own agents. The new Creative Agent is essentially an Adobe chatbot: You describe what you want, and the agent handles the execution in the appropriate app. It’s now in beta inside Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io.

All this makes it clear Adobe isn’t slowing down on AI. It has, however, recognized that a great bifurcation is taking place, one that’s affecting all industries to some extent, but especially the media. On the one hand, you have your AI skeptics, the customers who are suspicious of AI generally and AI-generated or -assisted content specifically. And on the other, you have the AI enthusiasts, the ones who are using AI to enhance and speed up their work, including through tools from other companies.

This is the AI tightrope, and all businesses will need to navigate it over the next few years. Not just because AI represents “the future” in some vague sense, but because, if it does, it opens up a new kind of customer.

Now everyone knows kung fu

My business is actually a pretty good example of this. I use various software, including Photoshop and Premiere, to help produce content like The Media Copilot podcast. But I’m not a creator per se, and I’m probably using only about 10% of the features that would help my use case. For many, that skill gap is the difference between subscribing and not. But an agent that bridges the gap could mean Adobe customers are no longer just enthusiasts and experts. Suddenly, we’re all Neo in the Matrix: Just plug an agent into your workstream, and you know kung fu. In fact, one of the Max keynote demos was more or less my exact workflow: an outside AI agent turning a long-form podcast into a batch of short clips for social media.

There’s also an urgency here, and again, my use case is a good example. I’ve already begun off-loading some of my production process to agents. Claude Code and OpenAI Codex are both excellent at analyzing workflows and recommending software solutions that they (not I) can operate. Often, it’s open-source software that gets the job done at virtually no cost other than the tokens I expend. And Adobe users can even employ computer use—in which the AI uses your machine, just as you would—to operate the software. It’s messier than an MCP, but it gets the job done, and AI is getting better at this by the day.

In other words, the AI world is moving toward agentic work, with or without Adobe. Businesses of all kinds are beginning to demand this kind of functionality, and even if open-source software is cheaper, there are advantages to using commercial software. Security, reliability, and auditability are all very important to enterprises. And it’s mutually beneficial to Adobe, since the number of licenses those businesses buy will no longer be limited by the number of experts they have. Notably, the MCP integrations require the apps to be installed and licensed on the user’s machine. Even when an agent is the one driving Photoshop, someone is still paying for the seat.

Media’s version of the same customer

There’s a corollary here in media. As people turn more and more to AI answers for information, it means bots scrape all kinds of sites to find the best possible answer. A consequence of this is that niche sites—in particular B2B media—have become some of the most sought-after sources on the web. TollBit’s latest “State of the Bots” report ranks B2B and professional sites among the most heavily scraped categories it tracks, with scraping up 62% from Q2 2025 to Q4 2025. 

Their specialized knowledge might sometimes be impenetrable to mainstream audiences, but never to AI agents. They can quickly parse the bits that are important and relevant, then break them down in a way that’s understandable to anyone. Just like with those Photoshop agents, lack of expertise is no longer a barrier to adoption.

But what about those AI skeptics? They’re an important part of any company’s existing customer base, and they’ve made their views clear: They don’t want to see AI in the content they consume. I’ve written about the problem with AI tells in text, and the same goes for images and video: Audiences consistently say they don’t like them. That doesn’t mean all AI is bad, and many Adobe AI-powered features garnered lots of applause at Max. But it needs to be in the right context. 

A good rule of thumb: AI behind the scenes is generally okay, but you need to be careful with generative content. The audience research lines up almost exactly. In the Reuters Institute’s “Generative AI and News Report 2025,” only 12% of people said they were comfortable with news generated entirely by AI, compared with 62% for news produced entirely by humans. But 55% were fine with AI fixing spelling and grammar.

Most media companies have arrived at a similar place. There are tantalizing opportunities for content to reach new audiences through AI search engines and agent protocols like MCP. At the same time, they need to tread lightly when implementing artificial intelligence in their own operations, lest they lose trust with their existing audience. That’s the AI tightrope, and staying balanced is obviously the trick to moving forward. 

Getting the agents to pay up

But what’s on the other end? At least for Adobe, the answer is clearer: a new and potentially huge customer base that doesn’t want to use tools but is happy for agents to. For media, the other end of the rope is murkier. The agents are already here, reading trade publications and national news alike, but most of them are still taking what they find without paying for it. AI apps send publishers a sliver of the traffic Google does, and the deals that would make up the difference are stuck in courtrooms and licensing negotiations.

Adobe found a way to charge for the agents using its tools. Until the media figures out how to get agents to pay for the privilege of reading content, it’s walking the same tightrope, just without a net.

#10808. RTO means women risk doing the office housework all over again

Women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all. Now, old-fashioned assumptions about the unpaid work women are expected to take on in the office risk adding to that burden.

Usually, the conversation about mental load centers on household chores, such as who is responsible for doing the laundry, planning meals, and buying the groceries. And it’s women who are more likely to do more domestic labor even when both partners are employed full time. One 2024 study of 3,000 US parents found that mothers took primary responsibility for 71% of household tasks requiring mental effort, compared with 45% for fathers. 

It happens at work, too, where it’s known as “office housework.” These are the unpaid, often unrecognized tasks that keep an organization running but rarely help the people doing them advance their careers. Women therefore can end up doing more work without getting any credit for it.

And RTO might be making things worse.

A study of 1,091 professional women in the US found that 31% reported experiencing everyday gender discrimination when working on-site, compared with 17% when working remotely. This included performing tasks that weren’t their responsibility. The results suggest that being physically present can expose women to more everyday gender discrimination and create more opportunities for these assumptions to surface.

The problem is also evident in the UK. In a new survey of 2,000 working women and men by advocacy group Co-operatives UK, 22% of women said they’d been asked to do paperwork outside their role, 21% had been asked to clean or tidy the office, and 20% had been asked to make coffee for senior leaders. Overall, nearly half (49%) of women said they’d been asked more than once to do something outside their role, such as making tea or booking a meeting room.

Women have been highlighting the problem on social media, sharing their experiences and how they push back against the assumption that they’ll take on these tasks.

One content creator, Alex Schudy, said she had noticed colleagues using what she described as “weaponized incompetence” to try to get her to take notes in meetings, often by throwing her a compliment to disguise it. In her video on TikTok, she said she let the “silence linger” when one colleague suggested she do it because her handwriting was neat and she was “organized.” She politely declined, explaining that she needed to focus on presenting her part of the meeting. Someone else was designated the notetaker instead.

Another creator, Anna Kennedy, described in a video how much office housework she had come to realise women were doing — from keeping track of action items and chasing colleagues to making sure feedback was acted upon.

“Things that keep the machine moving fundamentally, but are not rewarded or seen in a performance review,” she said. “I’m never, I swear to God, never seeing men doing this kind of work.”

As more employees settle back into office life, many hope there have been changes for the better, particularly around work-life balance and flexibility. But some of the oldest workplace habits seem stubbornly resistant to change, and it’s time women stopped being expected to pick up the slack. 

Ultimately, they shouldn’t have to spend their working days doing the jobs that keep everyone else organized, only to be left behind as everyone else speeds ahead.

Turns old Game Boy cartridges into a chiptune jukebox.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new device on Kickstarter claims to make Game Boy cartridges relevant again by playing soundtracks from your favorite classic Nintendo games. The Retro Song Bird is a box-shaped speaker that supports Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges, with support for over 1,900 games. Simply inserting a cartridge into the speaker gives you access to all soundtracks and sound effects, which can be controlled using onboard physical controls including next, previous, and volume.

The Retro Song Bird also comes with a 3.5mm stereo line-out and a USB Type-C port in case you want to connect to other audio equipment. According to the developer, it offers accurate, register-level sound emulation and can be used to sample and remix music from your Game Boy cartridges. It exposes all four audio channels (two square, wave, noise) as separate USB audio streams that can be imported into a DAW. This allows you to isolate individual melodies, waveforms, and sound effects from old games to create your own melodies. There’s even support for LSDj for playing saved chiptune tracks, while two Retro Song Bird units can be synced for DJ-style performances using Game Boy cartridges instead of traditional records.

In addition to playing retro video game soundtracks, the Retro Song Bird also supports the Game Boy Camera, allowing you to use it as a webcam offering a glorious 128×112 pixels resolution and 5 frames per second speed. Other features include the ability to back up and restore save files, ROMs, flash writable carts, and export any soundtrack or sound effect as WAV onto your PC. The listing also includes other abilities, including an Alarm Mode, a record of every cartridge you've ever plugged in, an open API for developers, and over-the-air updates.

The Retro Song Bird is currently available to back on Kickstarter, with the standard model starting at $79. The introductory $59 Early Bird offer has already sold out, while the developer is also offering a two-unit bundle for $150. Shipments are expected to begin in April 2027.

The developer notes that only a handful of hand-assembled prototypes currently exist and that the hardware and design still need some refinements. The project also faces potential manufacturing challenges, including component availability, finding suitable manufacturing partners, and producing injection-molded enclosures. Like any other Kickstarter campaign, delivery timelines are subject to change, and backers should be aware that there is no guarantee the finished product will ship as planned.

#10805. The future of live entertainment

Change is in the air. Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us.

Amid this profound transformation, our desire for experiences that are deeply human has never been greater.

Technology can do so much, including simulating interaction and placing nearly limitless entertainment at our fingertips. But it cannot fully replicate formative live entertainment moments like the collective anticipation before a performance or the emotional release of thousands of people experiencing the same unforgettable moment together.

Human beings are fundamentally social. We are drawn to one another and transformed by shared experience. Gathering is part of who we are. That fundamental human desire places us on the precipice of a cultural renaissance.

Throughout history, moments of mass disruption have repeatedly created the conditions for extraordinary periods of advancement in art, science, architecture, technology, and design. These moments force societies to question familiar assumptions and search for new ways to understand one another.

We are entering such a moment now.

In this emerging age of artificiality, human creativity will command a new premium. So will presence. The experiences we cannot download, automate, or predict will become more valuable precisely because they are real.

For designers (and any type of creative), this is an extraordinary opportunity. We have the ability—and responsibility—to shape the experiences that define the next era of culture.

4 IDEAS TO GUIDE THE NEXT ERA OF CULTURE

History demonstrates that people are remarkably resilient. When confronted with uncertainty or moments of radical change, we search for reasons to believe in what comes next, then adapt accordingly. What follows are four ideas that can help ensure this latest cultural renaissance is a period of meaningful transformation that unites people globally for a shared purpose: connection.

1. The importance of optimism 

That instinct remains powerful today. According to recent research from VML Intelligence, 69% of respondents regularly feel hopeful about the future. Beneath the anxiety surrounding technological and cultural change, optimism persists.

That optimism matters because hope rarely remains an individual emotion. People seek opportunities to express it collectively. Live entertainment gives physical form to that desire.

Watching Lionel Messi with his foot on the ball in the 90th minute of the FIFA World Cup, a stadium erupting in victory, a concert audience singing a chorus with Taylor Swift, or a theater falling completely silent at the same emotional moment reveals something profound. Emotion becomes amplified when it’s shared.

The most successful venues build anticipation and entice participation. They create the conditions for strangers to feel connected.

As optimism becomes a defining force in the next cultural era, the places that bring people together will become increasingly important expressions of collective possibility.

2. The return of real

The renewed interest in analog experiences is already visible across culture. Vinyl records, tapes, and physical media have returned to prominence. Film cameras and Polaroids are reappearing at concerts and celebrations. Tactile pursuits such as journaling and knitting are attracting new generations.

These behaviors are sometimes dismissed as nostalgia. But they represent something more consequential: a desire for agency and authenticity. It is a tangible connection in a world of infinite, algorithmically delivered content.

People want experiences they can touch and remember. They want the imperfect and the unpredictable. They desire the unrepeatable. Live entertainment is the ultimate expression of that desire.

No two performances are the same. No crowd produces the same energy. No professional athlete reacts in the same way in that critical winning moment. The possibility that something unexpected might happen is the source of its power.

Designers are beginning to respond through spaces that encourage deeper presence and participation. Listening rooms, intimate performance spaces, flexible venues, and carefully choreographed social environments are creating new ways to experience music and culture together.

In the age of artificiality, the real becomes rare. Rarity creates the ultimate value.

3. From experience to transformation

This cultural recalibration aligns with B. Joseph Pine’s concept of the transformation economy. This is the idea that people increasingly seek experiences that change them.

Businesses and institutions will increasingly be judged by what they provide and by whether the experiences they create feel meaningful and transformative. This is especially true in sports and live entertainment, where identity, ritual, and emotion are inseparable from the event itself.

The 2026 FIFA World Cup offered a powerful expression of this idea. Supporters traveled from across the globe not simply to watch soccer, but to participate in one of humanity’s great, shared traditions. The matches mattered, but so did the pilgrimage, the gathering, the rituals, and the sense of belonging to a global community.

The same principle exists at every scale, spanning the intimacy of a listening room to the collective roar of a stadium and everything in between. Each can become a place where human connection is forged, moments that become treasured memories.

4. A collective opportunity awaits

The next era of live entertainment will be defined by how thoughtfully technology is used to deepen, not displace, the human experience.

Our greatest opportunity is to design places that encourage people to look up from their devices, toward the performance and toward one another. Places that transform attendance into participation, audiences into communities, and fleeting moments into enduring memories.

These places give physical form to the things artificial intelligence cannot manufacture; chief among them, authentic, spontaneous, and shared emotion.

The conditions for a cultural renaissance are already here. Its character, however, is not predetermined. It will be shaped by the choices of many, including cultural and entertainment leaders. Let’s collectively embrace an opportunity to design and lead a new era. It’s one that doesn’t come often and can spark lasting impacts that will positively influence generations to come.

Brian Mirakian is senior principal at Populous.

#10804. Jensen’s exit could be Google’s TPU moment

Good morning. Today I’m rewatching Tenet to better picture Robert Pattinson in his new role, sighing over the inevitability of delivery drones triggering PTSD symptoms, and laugh-cringing at some of these Bit.ly link hijack stories from the weekend. Plus, prayers to anyone who had to find a last-minute hotel room during last week’s flying nightmare.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

In the immediate fallout of Jensen Huang’s humiliating resignation from Nvidia, coverage will focus on how the company plans to continue without its beloved former CEO, the world’s biggest champion of open-source AI and the proliferation of GPUs across borders. But in the long term, there’s an argument to be made that Google will be one of the largest winners of the shake-up, with a market opening up to competition outside of Nvidia’s CUDA moat.

While Colette Kress, the interim CEO, is unlikely to make any drastic changes to the company’s roadmap, the reality is that Nvidia’s competitors in the semiconductor space have desperately been working to unseat the market leader, and without Jensen at the helm, customers may be more likely to pursue alternatives.

For years, Google has offered its TPUs, or Tensor Processing Units, as a solution for AI training and inference, but they’ve been largely locked to its Google Cloud infrastructure. That’s changing now that the company is opening up sales to third parties and has announced it will bring TPU capacity to Oracle’s cloud beginning in 2027.

Google’s latest generation of TPUs is specialized; here’s how the company describes the lineup in its recent announcement post:

While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning (inference), TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

Google isn’t comparing its new TPUs directly to Nvidia’s offerings, and clock-for-clock, even the most powerful TPU 8i Max doesn’t touch Vera Rubin for sheer performance. But this generation should be much more competitive for a few reasons: it’s more power efficient in certain configurations, and Google made it easier to translate coding workflows optimized for CUDA to work with its TPUs.

Back in October, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, which it co-developed with Meta’s PyTorch team, to let developers use familiar PyTorch workflows on TPUs with minimal code changes. That won’t make every custom CUDA operation portable or eliminate performance tuning, but reducing the effort required to try an alternative may change the buying decision. Customers don’t need to abandon Nvidia outright for Google to increase its TPU market share, or for Nvidia to face more pressure on price.

Alongside Broadcom and MediaTek, Google is taking on the Nvidia behemoth, and in the short term, it will almost certainly see a large upside in sentiment. But in the longer term, with scaling pressure lowering margins for Nvidia, Google’s specialized and more efficient TPUs may be a primary beneficiary of this sea change. They could also offset a slowdown in Search as Google’s shift to Cloud continues apace.

Over the past few days, the one-two punch of Microsoft’s 365/Exchange outage and the FAA’s ground stop shows just how vulnerable everyone is to the effects of seemingly brittle tech infrastructure.

The FAA describes a flood of connection attempts that destabilized its telecommunications network, affecting aircraft communications and radar feeds. Investigators identified sites in Arkansas and Texas that were undergoing router and wire replacements, but even days after the stop was lifted, there’s still no clear underlying cause.

Meanwhile, the Microsoft 365 outage lasted about 30 hours, with service restored to the remaining customers and regions late Friday. Microsoft says that a “latent defect” introduced into its network code in a July update wasn’t triggered until a few days ago, when high loads led to cascading failures across the company’s servers worldwide.

While neither AI nor cyberattacks were to blame, individually and together the two outages add urgency to getting companies to shore up their defenses and redundancies in a world where we’re overly reliant on digital systems.

#10802. People are using Meta’s Muse to purge who they’re following on Instagram

Since the days of MySpace’s Top 8, social media has made it easy to hurt your friends’ feelings. Some platforms make it easy to judge relative friendship, like Snapchat’s publicly viewable “Best Friends” feature.

Instagram, however, keeps users’ social dynamics under wraps from one another, with accounts unable to see when someone unfollows them. Instagram head Adam Mosseri has previously said the platform hasn’t introduced a “who unfollowed me” feature so that users feel free to unfollow whomever they please without fear of judgment or tension.

But a new tool from Instagram’s parent company Meta is shaking things up. Its AI assistant Muse has an apparently petty personality under its cute and cuddly exterior—and it’s happy to help users spot who isn’t following them back and then unfollow them en masse.

How Muse can purge your Instagram

Social media users have discovered that Muse can sort through the people they follow on Instagram and point out any non-mutual connections. Though third-party apps have offered similar features in the past, they’re notorious for getting accounts flagged and taken down from Instagram. Muse, as an in-house app, doesn’t pose the same risk.

One Instagram user who tried out the feature, Khalil Roberts, told Wired about his experience using Muse. Roberts gave Muse the prompt, “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on Instagram, and can you unfollow them for me.” It quickly returned an Excel spreadsheet with 151 accounts that fit his criteria, then asked if he wanted to follow through on unfollowing them.

Roberts was among the chorus on social media singing Muse’s praises for letting them purge such accounts so easily. “I just cleared 80+ chopped hos who thought I was a fan,” one user posted.

“Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG,” another user boasted, crediting Muse in a follow-up post.

Meta’s secret menu

Though Muse’s potential for pettiness is a much-requested feature, it’s only being spread through word of mouth. Meta itself isn’t advertising the capability—or at least not anymore.

In October, Los Angeles-based social media consultant Rachel Karten noticed a Meta ad on Instagram touting that Muse could let users “see who unfollowed you each week.”

“I get that this is technically a requested feature but wouldn’t it lead to more resentment towards your own platform?” Karten asked in a post sharing a screenshot of the ad.

Indeed, Instagram has since taken down the ad, as a Meta representative confirmed to Business Insider. Still, the feature remains active in Muse—as long as users know to ask for it.

#10801. Google’s new ‘Fast Switch’ feature leaks, lets you use one number on two Android phones

Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.

A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and quickly switch devices on the fly.

Other strings explicitly say that you can “Use a SIM on two phones” and specify that both devices would need to be logged into the same Google account. One phone would be the “Primary” with the other as a “companion.”

There are still plenty of unknown details here, including what data might sync between devices as well as how carriers will respond. On iPhone, carriers either charge extra for this feature ($5 at T-Mobile, $10 at Verizon), or don’t support it at all (AT&T). We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

This would make my decision to buy device like Clicks Communicator much easier

As per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting.

iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

On Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?

#10800. When Should You Remove NAT from an On-Prem Kubernetes Network?

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

In an on-premises Kubernetes environment, removing NAT can make the network simpler to inspect, reduce translation overhead, and let the data center route directly to workloads. But direct routing is not automatically the right choice.

The decision depends on what the organization controls and what it needs from the network. A team that owns the physical fabric, has enough address space, and is comfortable operating BGP may benefit from making pod networks directly routable. A smaller environment, a team without control of the underlay, or a cluster that benefits from network abstraction may be better served by NAT or an overlay.

Kubernetes is also changing the ground under these decisions: kube-proxy is set to drop IPVS support starting with version 1.43, with nftables as the replacement. For on-prem teams already reviewing their service data path, it is a good moment to ask whether NAT still belongs in it.

So the useful question is not how to eliminate NAT, but when the operational benefits of doing so justify the additional routing responsibility.

NAT solves a real problem. It allows an internal network to use its own address space without requiring the surrounding infrastructure to know how to reach every endpoint inside it. This is especially useful when you don’t control the underlying network.

However, an on-premises data center is different. When you control both the Kubernetes cluster and the surrounding physical network, you can make Kubernetes networks directly routable.

In our case, removing NAT had practical and architectural benefits. It improved network performance, reduced CPU load on the nodes, and removed the risk of conntrack tables filling up on Kubernetes hosts. A directly routed L3 model also works well for traffic balancing when a node has two uplinks.

This does not mean eliminating NAT from the data center entirely. NAT can remain at the boundary of the on-premises network, for example on hardware firewalls. Inside the data center, however, Kubernetes networks can be directly routable, allowing the physical network to reach workloads using the same routing mechanisms it already uses elsewhere.

In our implementation, BGP connects the Kubernetes network to the data center fabric: BIRD runs on the nodes and advertises pod CIDRs and selected service addresses, while kube-router manages Kubernetes networking. We described this implementation in more detail in our earlier article on building a routable on-prem

Kubernetes cluster with BGP and ECMP. The important point for this decision is not the particular stack, but the requirement it creates: the surrounding network must be able to accept and route Kubernetes prefixes safely. If the organization cannot or does not want to make the cluster part of its routing domain, keeping NAT or an overlay is usually the simpler choice.

Removing NAT alone does not make a network resilient. If every node still depends on one switch, one NIC, or one uplink, direct routing simply exposes the same physical single point of failure more clearly.

The resilience benefit appears when the physical topology supports multiple independent paths. In our setup, nodes connect to independent data center switches and ECMP can use equivalent routes across those paths. If one path disappears, traffic can continue over the other.

That distinction matters when deciding whether direct routing is worth the effort. Organizations with redundant uplinks and switches can integrate Kubernetes into an already resilient routed fabric. If the underlay itself has no path redundancy, removing NAT should not be presented as a high-availability improvement: the physical failure domain still dominates the design.

Our stack is one example of how direct routing can be implemented, not a default recommendation for clusters that remove NAT. We chose kube-router because it supports a minimal installation as a binary and systemd service and covers the networking functions we need for this L3 design. BIRD handles route advertisements to the surrounding network.

Other environments may reasonably choose Calico for conventional L3 routing or Cilium when an eBPF-based dataplane and its additional capabilities are useful. The choice of CNI and routing daemon is secondary to the architectural decision: first decide whether exposing Kubernetes prefixes to the physical network makes operational sense, then choose the implementation that fits the team’s requirements.

A directly routed Kubernetes network is not automatically better than an overlay or NAT-based architecture. Each model solves a different operational problem.

NAT is a reasonable choice when the cluster needs to remain isolated from the surrounding address plan, when pod addresses cannot be routed through the data center, or when the infrastructure team does not control the upstream network. It also keeps Kubernetes-specific prefixes out of the physical routing domain, which can be valuable for smaller environments where direct visibility into every pod is not important.

An overlay is useful when portability and abstraction matter more than exposing the physical packet path. It lets Kubernetes networking remain largely independent of the underlay and can simplify deployment across heterogeneous infrastructure. The tradeoff is another layer to inspect during troubleshooting and, depending on the implementation, encapsulation overhead.

Direct routing makes the most sense when the organization owns the physical network, has address space available for pod CIDRs, and has operators comfortable with BGP and route filtering. It becomes more attractive when preserving source addresses, using standard network troubleshooting tools, predictable performance, or integrating the cluster with redundant data center paths are important. At a larger scale, those operational benefits can justify the extra coordination between Kubernetes and network teams.

The broader lesson is not that every Kubernetes cluster needs BGP or that NAT should disappear everywhere. It is that Kubernetes has matured enough that we should stop automatically treating its network as a black box.

As more production and AI workloads move onto Kubernetes, network architecture becomes part of application reliability. In an on-premises data center, BGP and ECMP give us the option to use the resilience already available in the physical network rather than building another isolated networking layer on top of it.

Sometimes the best way to make Kubernetes networking more robust is not to add another abstraction, but to remove one. But only when the surrounding infrastructure and the team operating it are ready to take responsibility for the routing that abstraction previously hid.

If most of those answers are yes, direct routing is worth serious consideration. If not, NAT or an overlay may be the more resilient operational choice—not because it is technically more advanced, but because it better matches the environment.

For the first time in its 33-year history, Nvidia on Tuesday reported quarterly financial results without Jensen Huang at its helm or on the call, after its cofounder and longtime chief executive departed five days ago. To no one's surprise, Nvidia continues to set new financial records as demand for its AI accelerators shows no signs of slowing down. The company reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter of its fiscal 2027, with its latest Vera Rubin platform generating $20 billion. Meanwhile, its supply commitments surged to $390 billion.

"Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," said Colette Kress, interim chief executive and chief financial officer of Nvidia. "Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater."

For the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on October 25, 2026, Nvidia posted revenue of $115.844 billion, an increase of 20% sequentially and 103% year-over-year. The company's net income reached $65.287 billion, up 105% from the same quarter last year, while gross margin hit 74.8%. Revenue from the Compute & Networking segment totaled $106 billion, up 20% quarter-over-quarter and 108% year-over-year. Meanwhile, the Graphics segment generated $9.8 billion, a sequential increase of 25% and 62% compared with the same period a year ago.

As expected, Nvidia's results during the quarter were primarily driven by its Data Center business, which generated $107.6 billion in revenue (and accounted for approximately 93% of the company's sales), up 21% sequentially and 110% YoY. Hyperscale customers accounted for $60.1 billion, an increase of 23% QoQ and 71% YoY, while sales to AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise customers reached $47.5 billion, up 18% sequentially and 195% compared to the same period last year. Although hyperscalers remain Nvidia's largest customer category, demand from AI cloud providers, industrial companies, and enterprises continues to grow considerably faster on an annual basis. Meanwhile, Edge Computing revenue reached $8.2 billion, up 14% sequentially and 42% year-over-year.

One of the main contributors to Nvidia's growth was its Vera Rubin platform, which generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, which Nvidia described as the fastest product ramp in its history. The company also reported strong demand for standalone Vera CPUs and continued sales growth for Blackwell Ultra. According to Nvidia, its hyperscale partners brought Vera Rubin systems into production in approximately one month, which is two times faster than the previous-generation Grace Blackwell platform.

"Vera Rubin is off to an extraordinary start: in its first quarter of production shipments, the Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue, making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history," Kress said. "We continue to see very strong demand for Vera and expect total CPU revenue to more than double in FY2028."

To support the expected growth of its AI infrastructure business, Nvidia has substantially increased its long-term procurement obligations. The company's supply and capacity commitments reached $390 billion at the end of Q3 FY2027, compared with $279 billion three months earlier and $119 billion at the end of Q1. Nvidia attributed the latest increase primarily to multiyear memory procurement agreements.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The company expects to fulfill $69 billion of these commitments during the remainder of FY2027 (which ends in late January), followed by $203 billion in FY2028 and $92 billion in FY2029. Another $26 billion is scheduled for FY2030 and beyond. In other words, Nvidia has already committed to purchasing $390 billion worth of components and manufacturing capacity through the end of FY2030, though given the fact that its purchases in FY2028 are set to exceed $200 billion, expect its procurements in FY2030 to be higher.

The commitments reflect Nvidia's efforts to ensure that its suppliers can manufacture sufficient quantities of advanced processors, memory, substrates, and packaging components. In addition to its existing agreements with partners like TSMC, Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, Nvidia on Wednesday announced new partnerships with Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Kinsus for substrates, as well as SPIL for advanced packaging. In addition, the company disclosed agreements with Amkor, Ibiden, KYEC, and Unimicron.

During the earnings call, Kress said that demand for Nvidia's products continues to exceed available supply, prompting the company to work with manufacturing partners to expand production capacity. She also indicated that Nvidia could provide suppliers with prepayments or other financial assistance to accelerate capacity expansion.

Although these procurement commitments are gargantuan, Nvidia expects demand for its AI infrastructure to remain strong, which will justify the expenditures. The company raised its revenue growth forecast for FY2028 from approximately 70% to 75% due to stronger demand and additional manufacturing capacity that it expects to secure.

In addition to its supply commitments, Nvidia disclosed $32 billion in agreements with neocloud providers that allow it to earn revenue from hardware sales and participate in cloud rental revenue above a guaranteed minimum. Meanwhile, the company's maximum financial exposure under various guarantees reached $118 billion, including $105 billion in credit support for the PORTS-Pike AI data center campus in Ohio, which will serve OpenAI under 20-year leases.

In total, Nvidia's commitments reached $540 billion as of early Q4 FY2024.

Nvidia currently absorbs higher component and manufacturing costs to honor existing purchase orders and maintain previously agreed prices for its customers. As a result, the company expects its GAAP gross margin to decline from 74.8% in Q3 FY2027 to 71% – 72% in Q4, which it considers the bottom of the current margin cycle.

Going forward, Nvidia plans to introduce revised pricing in FY2028 to help offset higher supply costs and restore profitability, which is when the company expects gross margins to recover to 72% – 73% next fiscal year, although it has not disclosed the magnitude of its planned price adjustments or the products they will affect.

"We thought about in terms of our prices and pieces of that, and a lot of the costs were some of the things that we absorbed in those numbers that we included," Kress said. "What we provided here in Q4 is our bottom. If you recall, that was our bottom as we honored many of the different POs that we had already received from our customers, and we just wanted to make sure that was held solid as we moved to a new pricing, as we moved into the new year."

Perhaps more importantly is that Colette Kress largely sidestepped the question about custom AI accelerators and their potential impact on Nvidia's pricing power. During the conference call, an analyst asked whether Nvidia would accept lower margins to protect its market share against custom AI accelerators developed by hyperscalers. The interim CEO avoided directly addressing whether competition from custom silicon could undermine Nvidia’s competitive position, leaving considerable room for speculation.

For the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, Nvidia projects revenue of approximately $130 billion ±3%, which would represent an increase of about 12% sequentially. The company expects GAAP gross margin of 71% to 72% and GAAP operating expenses of approximately $11 billion during the quarter. Nvidia’s forecast excludes Data Center compute revenue from China and accounts for an additional week in the quarter. While Nvidia expects its gross margin to decline during the Vera Rubin transition, Kress said that the company anticipates a recovery to 72% – 73% in FY2028.

#10797. America’s next quantum breakthrough: The factory floor

Building a quantum computing company has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist. Developing a new technology is one challenge. Figuring out how to manufacture it reliably, at scale, is another. And the second can be every bit as difficult as the first.

For years, the prevailing wisdom in technology was to focus on what you do best and outsource the rest. It made good business sense. Building manufacturing capacity is expensive, complicated, and often far removed from the work that inspired someone to start a technology company in the first place.

But that approach comes with a tradeoff. When you depend on someone else to manufacture your technology, you also depend on their capabilities, priorities, and timelines.

For an emerging industry like quantum information, those dependencies can become significant obstacles. And I believe they have implications well beyond any one company.

A LESSON WE’VE ALREADY LEARNED

The United States has seen what happens when technological innovation and manufacturing become separated.

American companies designed many of the advanced semiconductors powering today’s AI revolution, but much of the manufacturing capacity needed to produce them was developed overseas. That arrangement supported decades of innovation and economic growth. It also created dependencies that have become increasingly difficult to ignore.

Now, the U.S. is investing heavily in rebuilding domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity. It’s a difficult and expensive undertaking, and one that will take years to fully realize.

Quantum technologies give us an opportunity to think about these challenges earlier in an industry’s development.

The U.S. has extraordinary strengths in quantum science. Our universities, national laboratories, and private companies have helped advance the field for decades. But the path from a scientific breakthrough to a useful product requires more than research. Much more. It requires specialized materials, fabrication processes, engineering expertise, and the ability to produce increasingly complex technologies consistently and economically.

Those capabilities need to develop alongside science.

WHY WE CHOSE TO BUILD

I’ve experienced this challenge firsthand at Quantum Computing Inc. Our work in quantum photonics depends on highly specialized manufacturing processes. As we developed our technology, we had to think carefully about how much of our future we wanted to depend on outside manufacturing partners.

For a growing company, investing in your own manufacturing capabilities is a consequential decision. It requires capital, specialized expertise, and a willingness to take on responsibilities that extend well beyond research and product development.

We ultimately decided to build and acquire manufacturing capacity because we believe greater control over the critical and proprietary processes is essential to our long-term strategy. For other processes, we will leverage existing manufacturing capabilities and collaborate with industry partners to build a robust, reliable, and sustainable supply chain. 

We also see an opportunity to contribute to the broader ecosystem by making our manufacturing capabilities available to others. The quantum opportunity is far bigger than any one company.  Advancing the industry will require collaboration and shared capabilities that benefit all of us. It’s time to work together to build that foundation and accelerate the growth of the quantum industry.

NO ONE MANUFACTURING MODEL

That decision has shaped how I think about innovation.

When researchers and engineers have closer access to manufacturing, they can learn from what happens during fabrication and use that knowledge to improve the next design. Manufacturing becomes part of the development process itself. The experience gained along the way can be just as valuable as the equipment.

There is no single manufacturing model that makes sense for every quantum company. Different technologies have different requirements, and outside foundries and specialized partners remain important. But access to reliable manufacturing capacity can have a profound influence on how quickly an idea becomes something useful.

BUILD AN INDUSTRY, NOT JUST A TECHNOLOGY

Washington D.C. is beginning to recognize this challenge. A June executive order addressing quantum technology calls for strengthening domestic manufacturing capabilities and expanding partnerships between government and private industry.

I welcome that attention. But building a manufacturing base requires more than funding announcements and policy commitments. It takes facilities, equipment, specialized talent, and years of experience developing processes that work consistently. It also requires demand from companies that are ready to move technologies out of the laboratory and into practical use.

Other countries recognize the importance of these capabilities, with many having committed substantial resources to quantum technology. The United States has important advantages in research, entrepreneurship, and private investment. We should be building on those strengths now.

That doesn’t mean every component needs to be manufactured domestically. International partnerships and global supply chains will continue to play important roles. But we should be deliberate about which capabilities are essential to our technological independence, making sure we have the capacity to develop and sustain them.

FINAL THOUGHTS

I’ve spent much of my career working to advance quantum technology. Like many scientists, I was initially drawn to the possibilities of what we could discover and what those discoveries make possible.

Today, I spend just as much time thinking about what it takes to turn those possibilities into something people can use. That means manufacturing, supply chains, engineering, and all the difficult work that follows a breakthrough.

The U.S. has an extraordinary foundation in quantum science. What we do with that advantage now matters. We need to invest in the ability to manufacture these technologies with the same conviction and intensity we brought to discovering them.

Yuping Huang is CEO of Quantum Computing Inc.

#10796. The poster for the Sam Altman movie looks like AI slop. It’s actually brilliant marketing

The official movie poster for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming film about OpenAI, looks like AI slop, only it was drawn by human hands.

Anyone who has come across AI-generated images knows they often carry telltale mistakes. So when film studio Neon released the poster this week, users on social media were quick to catch oddities in the illustration, leading some to suspect it was made using AI.

At first glance, the poster looks normal.

On a closer look, Andrew Garfield, who plays Sam Altman in the movie, doesn’t appear quite like himself, lingering somewhere in the uncanny valley. The background features San Francisco’s landscape, except the Golden Gate Bridge is underwater. The tree behind Garfield looks distorted, with a Pinocchio-like face surfacing from the trunk. The branches are no less strange, morphing into snakes.

The closer you look, the weirder it gets.

Just a few hours after the poster was rolled out on social media, Neon followed up with a video showing a human drawing the scene by hand, crediting illustrator Mike Thompson and creative studio Gravillis.

“Art made by humans,” Neon captioned the behind-the-scenes video on X.

Users on social media quickly changed their tune, praising the studio and the movie’s creative team for their approach to the poster design.

“The poster for [Artificial] being made by an actual human artist while made to look like it was AI generated wow that’s luca GODagnino,” one user said on X.

Another user added, “This poster is a masterpiece. So many fun, completely bizarre, and purposeful ‘AI Slop’ touches. Zoom in and see if you can spot them all.”

Many also took notice that Neon didn’t just come out and say the poster was made by humans but rather made the effort to film a behind-the-scenes video and upload it as proof.

“Thank you for filming their processes and including the views of the artists in a world where what we see can be compromised or untrue,” one user said on X.

People-powered

Neon is not the first company to show how its work was made as a way to stand apart from AI slop. In recent months, brands across retail and tech have done the same.

In August, Apple released a behind-the-scenes video of its claymation ad for the new Mac Mini. Prada’s animated holiday campaign includes sketches from the artist.

But behind-the-scenes footage works only when the ads themselves are craft-forward, leaning on labor-intensive handwork as a form of effort signaling.

While proof of humanness taps into the film’s theme—bringing a sense of irony by making human art look artificial—not every observer is embracing the marketing trend.

One X user proclaimed, “Anybody posting any type of art now has to prove to morons that it was genuinely created by them and not AI. What a shit hole time period we live in.”

#10795. Samsung’s Galaxy S27 redesign is ‘100%’ confirmed, leaker says – do you like it? [Poll]

Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series is getting a redesign, with a reliable leaker saying it’s definitely happening. But, do you like it?

To say that Galaxy smartphone design has been stale is a bit of an understatement. The same core design has been in use for over half a decade at this point, with only the smallest tweaks in the past few generations. And it’s been a problem, too. While Samsung insists that the vertical triple camera array is the company’s “core identity,” it also means that the industry’s move to magnetic wireless charging and accessories are essentially incompatible with Galaxy devices.

We’ve seen repeated leaks of the Galaxy S27 series so far with a new full-width camera island on the Ultra and Pro models, and leaker Ice Universe says that this design is now “100%” confirmed, with the final design having two larger camera lenses on the left side, a smaller lens on the bottom right, and a flash above that. We saw this same design in a leak earlier this month, which Ice said at the time was “wrong,” presumably because the flash was replaced by a fourth camera in the dummy unit.

But the question at this point is, do you even like this new look?

Personally, I’m on the fence. I’m thrilled Samsung is finally doing away with the table-rocking, Qi2-ruining vertical array, but I’m not exactly happy we’re getting an iPhone clone as a result. I’d say beggars can’t be choosers, but this is Samsung we’re talking about – I think it’s fair to ask for a bit more.

#10791. AI adoption could disproportionately harm Black and Latino workers

It has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest. While entry-level roles are, in fact, on the decline in tech and finance—and employers continue to use AI as a rationale for layoffs—there is ample evidence that rapid AI adoption could interrupt pathways for workers without college degrees. 

The effects of this upheaval will be uneven, which means certain demographic groups are more likely to be impacted. Some of the jobs that have been deemed “highly exposed” to AI, including clerical and administrative roles, are largely dominated by women, and a new report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility posits that Black and Latino workers could also face major consequences.

The report finds that Black and Latino workers are overrepresented in the sectors where automation and AI adoption will supplant work altogether, rather than augment work. While the overall rate of AI adoption is relatively stable across different demographics, Black and Latino workers will be affected more acutely by job displacement. Across working hours that are impacted by AI adoption, 40% of hours performed by Black workers and 41% by Latino workers will be displaced (as compared to 37% among white workers). 

That may not seem like a huge gap. But as the report points out, many of the jobs that are most exposed to AI have historically been pathways to the middle class, making them crucial drivers of social mobility across communities that have faced systemic barriers to entry. Black workers, in particular, dominate six jobs that are likely to see the biggest decline in labor demand, according to McKinsey, including postal mail carriers and customer service representatives; Latino workers are also especially likely to hold some of those jobs, namely dishwashers and hand packers. 

Black and Latino workers—along with workers in rural regions—are also much more likely to be in jobs that involve physical labor, which are more vulnerable to being automated through robotics and other AI-enabled systems.

On the whole, lower-wage workers will face the greatest impact, and are 7.6 times as likely to need to transition into a new job when compared to higher-wage workers; people without a college degree are 1.8 times more likely to need to do the same. 

Meanwhile, white workers are better positioned to both avoid this level of AI disruption and actually benefit from AI adoption in a number of ways. It’s not just that they’re more likely to hold jobs where AI will enhance their work, boosting productivity rather than replacing employees outright. When compared to their Black and Latino counterparts, white workers are also 30% to 50% more likely to work in the industries where private capital will be deployed, yielding more jobs and wealth creation, the McKinsey report states. 

That means white workers already have more of a foothold in jobs involving robotics or semiconductors or biotech, setting them up for success as hundreds of billions of dollars pour into those industries. (Look no further than the Anthropic IPO this week, which has created thousands of millionaires.) 

In other words: Without broader policy changes or reskilling initiatives, many Black and Latino workers may be forced out of their jobs and locked out of opportunities to cash in on the AI boom.

#10790. XREAL Aura Initial Review: Taking Android XR out of the headset, but who is it for?

We all kind of want to be Tony Stark, don’t we? Almost everyone can relate to that futuristic sense of wonder that comes from the movies where we see digital elements being interacted with through a simple wave of the hand. To date, that’s only really been replicable through big ol’ headsets like Apple’s Vision Pro or the various Meta Quest sets. But with XREAL Aura, Android XR brings that feeling to something far easier to actually use, but my one remaining question is who this product is for.

XREAL isn’t new to the mixed reality space. The company has been building some of the best example of optical see-through XR glasses. These aren’t quite like a VR headset because they actually let you see the world around you, not through a camera, but by simply making the lenses themselves see-through. I’ve tried these in the past and, while they’re great for mirroring a tablet or laptop for bigger screen (especially on airplanes), I did feel they were missing something.

The other half of the formula is a wired puck that provides battery power and the brains of Android XR. There’s no screen on the puck, just a status light, and it has USB-C out for the glasses as well as USB-C in for power and/or external devices. It also has a fingerprint sensor (are you hearing this Android tablet makers??) and a touchpad, the latter used as a secondary, far subtler input method within Android XR to supplement hand tracking.

Together, these two make a wonderful package for building a true mixed reality experience. The displays are plenty bright for even the brightest indoor conditions (frankly, it’d be insane to use these outside in my opinion, though a wide-open plane window may present a challenge), and the electrochromic dimming does a great job of blocking out most, but not quite all of the world around you. If you’re looking to be fully cut off from reality as you would with a VR headset, these aren’t for you. I did find some display elements, like smaller text, a little tough to focus my eyes on at times, but I have a feeling that’s more so me being overdue for an eye exam than it is the glasses themselves. There’s virtually no flicker in my usage, with only bright white backgrounds occasionally being a little overbearing, and everything is smooth with the 120Hz refresh rate.

Where this hardware really shines compared to a typical VR headset is in its design, and it’s what makes XREAL a perfect partner for Android XR. The glasses themselves weigh in at 95 grams, a mere fifth of the Meta Quest 3 and Samsung’s Galaxy XR, and up to 700 grams less than Apple’s Vision Pro. It’s comfortable for much longer periods of time and not nearly as annoying to actually put on either, as it just feels like putting on a pair of bulky sunglasses. They look a little goofy, obviously, but far less so than a full-on VR headset like any of those mentioned above. This is also the only one of those I consider “mixed reality” thanks to the see-through lenses. Apple and Samsung constantly talk about Vision Pro and Galaxy XR as if they’re mixed reality, but a camera feed is explicitly not true reality. But XREAL’s glasses still aren’t quite just augmented reality, because they’re not just letting you see that digital world through a tiny window, they’re quite literally overlaying everything on top of the real world around you. The illusion is somewhat broken by the limited 70-degree field-of-view and the fact that darker backgrounds often look a little funky when there are light sources in the real world in front of you, but I can say with confidence that this is my favorite version of this experience – the speakers are pretty good too, topping it all off.

Google’s platform launched on Samsung’s Galaxy XR headset earlier this year, and it’s all pretty familiar on XREAL Aura. The Android-based experience opens up to a floating launcher of your favorite apps that mostly open up into floating windows in front of you. You can use hand gestures to move everything around or interact with UI elements, and every app I tried worked perfectly well. The gestures can be hit or miss at times, especially the one for going back to the home screen (having this as a long-press that you have to physically look at your hand for gets annoying when doing anything remotely fast-paced, but thankfully the top button is a dedicated home shortcut), but it works well and everything is designed fairly intuitively. A floating cursor shows where you are aiming with a pinch acting as a tap on a touchscreen, and you can move things around in your space as if they’re real objects. There’s a sense of depth throughout the entire experience.

Some apps open to fully immersive experiences, but these are still in the minority. XREAL touts that there are around 150 experiences launching alongside Aura, but it’s definitely still early days here. Apps like Google TV should obviously be ready for a full format like that but, most things, like the Google Docs app which I’m typing this review in right now, just act as if they’re on independent displays floating around you.

Like Googlebook, Android XR is also still struggling to figure out the best app experience for each user. Most things are mobile apps, including Google Chrome which is just the standard Android version from your phone. It’s fine in most cases, but I found this restrictive seeing as I can get a ton done in a browser, but fighting mobile optimization is a frustrating way to interact with a window that can be as big as a TV if you want it to. Meanwhile, the Spotify app is weirdly the web version which is horribly optimized for interacting with hand gestures. I’d have rather had the mobile version here. Another quirk I found was notifications, which pop up at the top of the display and quite literally on top of whatever you’re doing. Something they were invasive, and having to physically reach out to dismiss them is a little annoying. I’m sure there are workflows to help make this less of a distraction, but I’d almost rather have notifications turned off entirely.

There’s also Gemini, which is core to the experience here. A quick “Hey Google” triggers a Gemini Live session for answering questions, and you can share what you’re seeing to give additional context. It’s way faster than switching between apps to get a quick search done, but there are friction points here, especially if you’re just asking a single question. Gemini answers quickly and leaves the conversation going, great for follow-up queries, bad if you’re done because the UI controls go away, which leaves you to tell Gemini to end the session which, every time, it asks for secondary confirmation you want to end. Google, if I say “end the session,” I think that should be more than sufficient proof I want to end the session. Luckily, a long-press of the top home button fixes that headache, but I still hate that I either need to use a physical control, or basically have to fight an AI to end a conversation that I started hands-free.

Performance is excellent. Everything is smooth and quick, probably thanks in part to XREAL’s use of 12GB of RAM alongside Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite chip.

But how do you actually use a product like this?

That’s the question I found myself asking when I first spun up XREAL Aura and started to learn its ins and outs. See, other XREAL glasses have an extremely straightforward use case. Plug in the external device of your choice, get it on a bigger screen. Simple, easy, obvious. I found this helpful in travel primarily, with a bigger display for my MacBook feeling nice for tasks like video editing, while the main value came in just having a very comfortable way to watch a movie on a flight from my connected tablet.

Both of those use cases are valid on XREAL Aura. You can plug a USB-C device into the puck to get that wired mirroring through an Android XR window, and it works super well. Having Android XR alongside that mirroring also opens the door to added functionality, like having extra windows off to the side for perhaps a media app or reference document if you run out of room on the wired device. As just one example, I kept Spotify and Slack open in side windows while using Aura with my MacBook Air for an afternoon of writing articles.

I think Android XR makes Aura an absolute powerhouse for media consumption, as you can just download content directly to the device (256GB of storage in the base model) for a flight, or even just use streaming apps if you have Wi-Fi. I couldn’t find any 3D content during my brief review period (nothing in my Google TV library was compatible, apparently), but that’s also on the table. Genuinely, I cannot wait to use these on my next long flight.

But outside of those, I think a lot of the other scenarios start to fall apart.

By far the most popular use case for virtual/mixed reality has been gaming. XREAL Aura has a ton of potential here and I’m really excited to try out Project Hail Mary: Journey to the Stars on this, but the fact that these are simply glasses restricts a lot of what you can do. Any big movements could easily result in the glasses slipping or even falling off, whereas a VR headset is much more secure. Stationary immersive gaming has potential, and XREAL’s Gamesir controller collab shows promise, but I’m just not sold on these as a replacement to something like Meta Quest seeing as the latter already has a deep catalog of games and a much more affordable price.

The other use case is productivity, one I’m also not entirely sold on. As mentioned, this entire post was written in Aura, and I’m not sure I benefitted much from that experience versus just using a normal laptop or desktop computer. My workflow was having Google Docs up in the center, typing on a physical keyboard (only a psycho could use the virtual keyboard for anything beyond the shortest messages or passwords) with reference documents in Chrome off to my right and Slack on my left, with the occasional “Hey Google” command helping to find information on the fly (such as the weight comparison earlier). It all works well, but I think Android XR is inherently limited by its reliance mostly on mobile apps, and also just by the use of gestures. You can use a mouse or trackpad, of course, but at that point you might as well just use a laptop.

XREAL Aura is for a very specific customer from my point of view. Wired mirroring is still very much the strong suit here, with Android XR’s apps and offline video giving these utility outside of just relying on another device. That was my problem with previous XREAL glasses, because the experience just varies wildly depending on what’s connected. Aura’s puck and Android XR experience solves every complaint I had about previous models, while expanding very much on what it can do.

Further limiting matters is the price. $1,279, in my book, is actually a mostly fair price for this, especially given the RAMageddon of it all. XREAL 1+ Pro come in around $600 and is utterly useless without a secondary device. XREAL Aura more or less doubles the price, but includes the best possible version of that secondary device while also giving you the added camera sensors that are only available as add-ons for other hardware. Don’t get me wrong, it’s still pricey, but I don’t think it’s unfair either, especially not when one of the main competitors for this sort of experience is still $3,600 (which still sounds insane two years later, even for Apple).

We’ll have far more to say about XREAL Aura in a long-term review from our Nick Sutrich, but the verdict on day one is that Android XR has really solved the biggest problem for XREAL, while XREAL has solved a lot of big problems for Android XR, all while being an overall win for the user at the end of the day. Not so often we get a storybook ending like that in tech anymore, and I’m all here for it.

Don’t forget, XREAL Aura is $200 off – so $1,099 – through the end of December. Much more worth it at that price.

#10789. ‘The Hunger Games’ are back: Haymitch Abernathy can teach the C-suite about reluctant leadership

Around the office today, you might hear: “May the odds be ever in your favor.” After the tumultuous technical failures of the past week, the phrase might come off as alarming, but it’s actually a Hunger Games reference.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters today and tells Haymitch Abernathy’s origin story. Abernathy is an unlikely hero forced into leadership in the rebellion by circumstances out of his control.

This doesn’t mean the C-suite can’t learn a thing or two from him. Here are a few quick stats on the franchise and some of Haymitch’s best management lessons.

The Hunger Games franchise by the numbers

The Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins, the first book in the original trilogy, was published by Scholastic on September 14, 2008. It was followed by Catching Fire in 2009 and Mockingjay in 2010.

Before the second book even came out, Lionsgate acquired the film rights for the first book. It was a smart move because the four Hunger Games films have collectively made more than $1.45 billion at the domestic box office.

Collins took a break after the first trilogy. A stand-alone prequel novel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, came out in 2020, telling the backstory of Coriolanus Snow. The 2023 film version made more than $166 million at the domestic box office.

Sunrise on the Reaping was published in 2025. According to Deadline, the new film is expected to make at least $80 million at the domestic box office on opening weekend alone.

Haymitch Abernathy: Reluctant leader archetype

Haymitch Abernathy, played by Woody Harrelson in the original films and Joseph Zada in Sunrise, is an unconventional leader. He would rather be drinking away his sorrows than changing the fate of Panem—but sometimes management is thrust upon us.

Abernathy excels at strategic planning. In the original books and movies, he is able to guide Peeta and Katniss through the games two times while organizing a rebellion right under the Capitol’s nose. This comes through very careful planning and deception.

In the real world, however, business leaders need to be able to communicate a clear vision and how to execute it.

Abernathy is rough around the edges—and his tough exterior allows him to work with a diverse range of difficult colleagues to get results. You could call him a people-first strategist. For instance, he was able to get through to Katniss and help her play the public relations game by pretending to have feelings for Peeta. She did that so well that her love for him ended up becoming real.

In addition, Abernathy got the vain people of the Capitol to empathize with Katniss and Peeta and send them lifesaving supplies like medicine and water.

Plan, collaborate, and adapt

Similarly, managers will have to work with many different personalities, departments, or vendors. True leaders can approach each individual or organization in a way that uplifts their strengths.

Back in Panem, all this planning doesn’t mean the reluctant Abernathy can’t adapt. He thrives under pressure. He was the victor of the 50th Hunger Games, the Second Quarter Quell. He had to compete against 47 other tributes, double the usual amount. He won by using the force field around the arena against his opponent.

In business, as in the Hunger Games, not everything is going to go according to the five-year-plan. Sometimes you have to improvise solutions as problems arise.

As it hits theaters, Sunrise will reveal more of Abernathy’s story and administrative prowess. The business world should take note.

#10787. 7 Best Accounts Receivable (AR) Software Platforms for Automating Invoice-to-Cash

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The best accounts receivable software for your company is the layer that closes the stage where your cash leaks. If buyers settle from an emailed link and outreach starts late, a reminders tool covers most of it. If customers prefer to pay online by card or ACH, add a payments network with a customer portal. If clients require invoice uploads to Coupa or Ariba and clear multiple invoices with one blank-memo wire, you need an AR automation layer on top of the ERP. Every platform listed here serves B2B businesses invoicing other companies, excluding consumer payment apps and collection agencies.

Our source material is each vendor's public product, integration, security and pricing pages, plus G2 reviews, as they stood in November 2026.

About three in five US suppliers let business clients pay within 30 days, per Atradius's 2026 US payment practices survey (September 2026). Most overdue invoices settle within a month past due, so funds arrive roughly two months post-billing. The same survey notes US enterprises often lose 1% to 2% of B2B invoices to bad debt. Software that shortens this window performs four main functions:

What invoice-to-cash software does not handle is core billing operations. Billing schedules, revenue recognition, and GL accounting remain within the ERP. Contract-first platforms initiate workflows from signed agreements and map customer billing prior to collection efforts; invoice-first applications pick up after ERP invoice generation.

Most finance stacks have four layers: the ERP that creates the invoice and holds the books, a payments network, a reminders tool, and an AR automation layer working the steps in between.

The ERP covers the last row, and a reminders tool covers timing. The rows in between depend on reading what a customer or a portal sent, which is AR automation work. That share keeps growing. Paper checks fell to 26% of B2B payments in 2025, per the AFP 2025 Digital Payments Survey as reported by Nacha, and FedNow settled about 2.5 times as many payments in Q3 2026 as a year earlier, per Federal Reserve FedNow statistics. Heading into 2027, more money arrives over electronic rails while its remittance detail lands somewhere else.

On Xero or QuickBooks with customers paying from the emailed link, the leak tends to be timing, and a reminders tool covers it. Once W-9 requests and payment questions fill your team's week, the replies need a different layer.

Portal rejections and lump-sum wires put the leak in the table's middle rows, where an AR automation layer on the ERP fits. In a demo, we'd ask each vendor to show how fast its software flagged a rejected portal invoice, then to apply a multi-invoice wire with a blank memo live.

If your team still keys card numbers or chases ACH details, start with the payments layer. A payments network with a customer portal gives buyers stored methods and autopay. Unless the vendor says otherwise, it won't read replies or file into buyer portals, so plan an AR layer for those stages.
